summaryEn: It spent a decade turning an LED leadframe stamping business into the maker of the metal lid that carries heat away from AI accelerators. Revenue is accelerating toward +58% — and first-quarter earnings were flat, at a share price of NT$3,370 and twenty-three times book.
model: editorial (truth-audited: FinMind + press; thermal framing — the leadframe-to-heat-spreader transformation, position with a US GPU maker, Dayuan expansion and EPS/dividend compounding credited, but the central tension stated plainly: 2026Q1 EPS was flat year-on-year while monthly revenue accelerated to +58%, at 93.2× earnings and 23.34× book; analyst 2026 forecasts explicitly labelled as estimates, and the design-revision risk to heat-spreader pricing included; sector 電子工業 → Thermal Solutions)

sections.bodyMarkdown:
Jentech Precision (健策精密工業, TWSE: 3653) makes the metal that takes heat off a chip. Its core product is the **heat spreader** — the flat lid bonded over a processor die that conducts heat into whatever cools it — and around that it has built **microchannel liquid cooling, integrated package lids and IGBT liquid-cooling modules**. Founded in **1987** and **listed in November 2009**, it spent most of that history stamping **LED leadframes**, and roughly a decade converting itself into a semiconductor thermal supplier. It is described in industry coverage as the **main heat-spreader supplier to a US-based GPU maker**.

The transformation has produced remarkable numbers. Annual EPS ran **NT$20.37 (FY2022) → 16.55 (FY2023) → 24.15 (FY2024) → NT$36.76 (FY2025)**. Gross margin sits at **41.8%** and operating margin at **32.0%** — extraordinary for a metal-forming business, and the clearest evidence that this is a specified, qualified component rather than a machined part. **Trailing return on equity is 24.96%**, the balance sheet carries only a **29.4% debt ratio** with **NT$10.25bn of cash**, and **operating cash flow of NT$1.54bn exceeded NT$1.40bn of net income**. Dividends have compounded from **NT$6.0 (FY2021) to NT$21.72 (FY2025)**.

Demand is accelerating. Monthly revenue has run **+29%, −15%, +19%, +27%, +38% and +58%** over the last six months, and high-end heat spreaders began **small-volume shipment in 2025Q4** as a driver for the second half of 2026. The **Dayuan plant expansion across 2025–2027 raises total floor area by about 30%**, for high-end spreaders and IGBT liquid-cooling modules.

**And here is the tension that defines the investment case.** Despite that revenue acceleration, **2026Q1 EPS of NT$9.53 was essentially flat against NT$9.59 a year earlier**. Revenue is growing far faster than profit. Meanwhile the shares trade at **NT$3,370 — 93.2× earnings and 23.34× book**, with a **0.64% yield**. That is among the most demanding valuations in this collection, on earnings that did not grow last quarter.

Analyst forecasts circulating for 2026 — revenue of **NT$27.44bn and EPS up to NT$52.1** — are **analyst estimates, not company guidance**, and are presented here as such. Industry coverage also flags a specific risk worth taking seriously: **revisions to AI thermal design could correct the premium currently earned on high-basis heat spreaders.**

The honest read: **a genuinely successful transformation into a scarce, high-margin AI component — where revenue growth is real, profit growth has paused, and the price assumes neither.**

Jentech was founded in **1987** doing precision metal stamping, and for most of its life its main product was the **LED leadframe** — the stamped metal frame that holds an LED die and carries current and heat away from it. It was competent, unremarkable work in an industry that, as **Everlight (2393)** elsewhere in this collection documents, was subsequently commoditised by Chinese capacity. The company **listed in 2009**.

The reinvention took about a decade, and it started from a simple observation: **the leadframe's real job is thermal and electrical, and the same competence applies to far more valuable parts.** A **heat spreader** — the integrated heat spreader, or IHS, bonded over a processor — is a precision-formed metal lid whose flatness, thermal conductivity, plating and dimensional tolerance determine how effectively heat leaves the silicon. Get it slightly wrong and the processor throttles.

That mattered increasingly as chips got hotter, and then it mattered enormously. **AI accelerators dissipate several times the power of conventional processors**, concentrated in packages that keep growing. Thermal performance became a limiting factor on what a chip could be allowed to do, and the components that manage it moved from commodity hardware to qualified, designed-in parts. Jentech had spent years building exactly that capability, and became the **main heat-spreader supplier to a US-based GPU maker**.

The company has since extended along the thermal path rather than diversifying away from it: **microchannel liquid cooling**, where coolant runs through channels machined close to the die; **integrated package lids** combining spreading and mounting; and **IGBT liquid-cooling modules** for power electronics. **High-end heat spreaders entered small-volume shipment in 2025Q4**, and the **Dayuan plant is being expanded across 2025–2027, adding about 30% more floor area**.

The financial result is a business that looks nothing like a stamping company: **41.8% gross margin, 32.0% operating margin, 24.96% return on equity**, and a dividend that rose from **NT$6.0 to NT$21.72** in four years.

- **1987 (28 March)** — Jentech Precision Industrial founded, doing precision metal stamping — principally **LED leadframes**.
- **2009 (18 Nov)** — **Lists on the Taiwan Stock Exchange (3653)**.
- **2010s** — Begins a decade-long shift from LED leadframes into **semiconductor thermal components**, centred on **heat spreaders (IHS)**.
- **2020s** — Becomes the **main heat-spreader supplier to a US-based GPU maker** as AI accelerator power dissipation makes thermal performance a limiting factor. Extends into **microchannel liquid cooling, integrated package lids and IGBT liquid-cooling modules**.
- **2021** — Dividend **NT$6.0**.
- **2022** — **FY2022 EPS NT$20.37**; dividend nearly doubles to **NT$11.66**.
- **2023** — A softer year: **FY2023 EPS NT$16.55**; dividend **NT$9.85**.
- **2024** — Recovery: **FY2024 EPS NT$24.15**; dividend **NT$14.5**; Q4 gross margin **37.7%**.
- **2025Q4** — **High-end heat spreaders and thermal solutions begin small-volume shipment**, identified as the driver for the second half of 2026.
- **2025** — **FY2025 EPS NT$36.76**, up 52%; gross margin peaks at **44.9%** in Q1; dividend raised to **NT$21.72**.
- **2025–2027** — **Dayuan plant expansion** raising total floor area about **30%**, for high-end heat spreaders and IGBT liquid-cooling modules.
- **2026Q1** — **EPS NT$9.53 — flat against NT$9.59** a year earlier, despite gross margin of **41.8%** and operating margin of **32.0%**.
- **2026 (to June)** — Monthly revenue accelerates: **+29%, −15%, +19%, +27%, +38%, +58%**. Shares trade at **NT$3,370 — 93.2× earnings, 23.34× book**.

Jentech's accounts show **an exceptional manufacturer with an exceptional valuation, and one quarter that did not follow the revenue**.

- **Earnings compounding, until recently.** Annual EPS: **NT$20.37 (FY2022) → 16.55 (FY2023) → 24.15 (FY2024) → NT$36.76 (FY2025)** — a **52% rise** in the latest year. Then **2026Q1 delivered NT$9.53 against NT$9.59** a year earlier: **flat**.
- **The divergence that matters.** Monthly revenue over the same period ran **+29%, −15%, +19%, +27%, +38%, +58%** — accelerating sharply. **Revenue is growing far faster than profit.** The most likely explanations are mix (early high-end shipments at start-up cost), expansion expense ahead of the Dayuan capacity, or pricing. Whichever it is, the gap between a **+58% revenue month** and **flat quarterly EPS** is the single most important thing to watch.
- **Margins are outstanding and stable.** Gross margin: **37.7% (2024Q4) → 44.9% → 41.5% → 39.0% → 41.2% → 41.8% (2026Q1)**. Operating margin: **27.6% → 32.0%**. Net margin **26.5%**. For a company forming metal, this is closer to a semiconductor designer's profile than a manufacturer's, and it reflects a qualified, designed-in position.
- **A clean balance sheet.** **NT$30.31bn of assets** on **NT$21.40bn of equity** — a **29.4% debt ratio**, among the lowest in this collection — with **NT$10.25bn of cash**. **2026Q1 operating cash flow of NT$1.54bn exceeded NT$1.40bn of net income**, so the earnings are cash.
- **A dividend compounding fast.** Cash dividends (FinMind, by fiscal year): **NT$2.0 (2016, 2017) → 3.53 → 5.0 → 6.0 (2020, 2021) → 11.66 (2022) → 9.85 (2023) → 14.5 (2024) → NT$21.72 (2025)**. The **0.64% yield** is negligible only because the share price has risen far faster.
- **The valuation is the crux.** **NT$3,370 a share — 93.2× earnings and 23.34× book** on a **24.96% return on equity**. A price-to-book above 23 for a metal-forming business embeds many years of continued growth, and **2026Q1's flat EPS did not deliver any of it**.
- **On the analyst forecasts.** Estimates of **NT$27.44bn of 2026 revenue and EPS up to NT$52.1** are circulating in Taiwanese coverage. These are **analyst projections, not company guidance**, and should be treated accordingly.

The financing reality: **a debt-light, cash-generative business with genuinely rare margins — priced as though the last four years' growth rate is a permanent feature, in a quarter when it stopped.**

**Stance: the heat spreader supplier to AI accelerators, with 41.8% gross margins, 24.96% ROE and almost no debt — at 93x earnings and 23x book, on a quarter when earnings were flat.**

The bull case:

1. **A qualified position in a genuine bottleneck.** **AI accelerators dissipate several times the power of ordinary processors**, and thermal performance limits what a chip can be allowed to do. Jentech is the **main heat-spreader supplier to a US-based GPU maker** — a designed-in, qualified position rather than a machining contract.
2. **The margins prove it.** **41.8% gross, 32.0% operating, 26.5% net** on formed metal. Nothing about stamping produces those numbers; specification and qualification do.
3. **Demand is accelerating.** Monthly revenue reached **+58%**, **high-end heat spreaders started shipping in 2025Q4** for a second-half 2026 ramp, and the **Dayuan expansion adds about 30% of floor area** through 2027 for spreaders and IGBT liquid-cooling modules.
4. **Financially immaculate.** **29.4% debt ratio**, **NT$10.25bn cash**, **operating cash flow above net income**, dividends up from **NT$6.0 to NT$21.72** in four years, **ROE 24.96%**.

The counter-arguments:

- **Profit did not follow revenue.** **2026Q1 EPS of NT$9.53 against NT$9.59** while monthly revenue ran up to **+58%**. Whatever the cause — mix, start-up cost, pricing — a company at 93× earnings needs earnings to grow.
- **The valuation is extreme.** **93.2× earnings and 23.34× book** with a **0.64% yield**. There is no margin of safety and no income while waiting.
- **Design risk is specific, not theoretical.** Coverage flags that **revisions to AI thermal design could correct the premium** on high-basis heat spreaders. Packaging and cooling architectures are changing quickly; a shift toward direct-to-die or integrated cooling would alter what a spreader is worth.
- **Customer concentration.** Being the main supplier to one large GPU maker is the strength and the exposure.
- **The 2026 forecasts are analysts', not the company's.**

A **bottleneck-at-a-price** thesis: an excellent, genuinely scarce business — where the entire question is whether the earnings resume growing fast enough to justify what has already been paid.

Jentech makes **precision metal parts whose job is to move heat**, and its economics come from being specified rather than quoted:

- **Heat spreaders (the core).** The integrated heat spreader is the metal lid bonded over a processor die. Its **flatness, thermal conductivity, plating, warpage behaviour and dimensional tolerance** determine how efficiently heat leaves the silicon and reaches the cooler above. For a large AI accelerator dissipating enormous power across a big package, small deviations translate directly into throttling — which is why the part is qualified into a design and not re-tendered casually.
- **Liquid cooling and integrated lids.** **Microchannel liquid cooling** runs coolant through channels formed close to the die, and **integrated package lids** combine spreading with mounting hardware. Both raise content value per package and move Jentech further into the thermal system rather than a single component.
- **IGBT liquid-cooling modules.** The same competence applied to power electronics — a separate end market with its own cycle, supported by the Dayuan expansion.
- **The legacy business.** **LED leadframes**, the company's original product, now a small and commoditised part of the mix.
- **Why the margin is 41.8%.** Not because metal forming is profitable — it is not — but because a **qualified thermal component in an AI accelerator is chosen on performance and supply reliability**. The customer's cost of a thermal failure vastly exceeds the part's price, so the part is not bought on price.
- **Where the capacity comes from.** The **Dayuan plant expansion across 2025–2027 adds roughly 30% of floor area**, aimed at high-end spreaders and IGBT modules — expansion into demand the company cannot currently serve.

The levers are **AI accelerator volumes, content value per package, mix between standard and high-end spreaders, and utilisation of the new capacity**. The strength is a designed-in position in a component whose importance rises with every increase in chip power, funded from a **29.4% debt ratio** with **cash flow above profit**.

The vulnerability is specific and worth stating: **thermal architecture is changing fast**. Direct-to-die cooling, integrated cold plates and new package designs all alter what a heat spreader does and what it is worth — which is precisely the "design revision" risk that industry coverage identifies, and a plausible part of why **revenue grew while 2026Q1 profit did not**.

Thermal management became a first-order semiconductor problem when AI accelerators stopped being able to shed their own heat.

- **Why it became a constraint.** A conventional server processor dissipates a few hundred watts. **AI accelerators dissipate multiples of that**, in packages that keep growing to accommodate more silicon and stacked memory. Once heat cannot be removed fast enough, the chip throttles — so **thermal performance limits computational performance**, and the components that manage it become gating items rather than accessories.
- **The stack of solutions.** Closest to the die sits the **heat spreader (IHS)**; above it, thermal interface material, then a **cold plate or heat sink**; then the system-level solution — air, liquid or immersion cooling. Value has been migrating **down the stack toward the die**, because that is where the thermal bottleneck actually is. Jentech's move into **microchannel liquid cooling and integrated lids** follows exactly that migration.
- **The competitive set.** Taiwanese thermal companies including **Auras, Sunon and AVC** compete more in modules, heat pipes and fans; Jentech's position is nearer the package. Its qualification with a **US-based GPU maker** is the differentiating asset, and one that took years.
- **The AI infrastructure chain in this collection.** Jentech sits alongside **Elite Material (2383)** in high-speed laminate, **Taiwan Glass (1802)** in low-dielectric glass cloth, **King Slide (2059)** in server rails, **Wiwynn (6669)** in servers and **Shihlin Electric (1503)** in data centre power. All are driven by the same hyperscaler capital cycle, and all would feel a pause in it together.
- **The technology risk that is specific to this layer.** Packaging and cooling architectures are being redesigned continuously — **direct-to-die cooling, integrated cold plates, new lid geometries**. Coverage of Jentech specifically flags that **design revisions could correct the premium** currently earned on high-specification spreaders. Unlike a materials shortage, this risk is not resolved by adding capacity; it is resolved or created by what the chip designers decide.

Jentech's position is **strong and technically earned**. The industry truth is that **thermal components close to the die are valuable precisely because the architecture around them is unsettled** — which makes today's premium real, and makes it contingent on design choices Jentech does not make.

**Strengths**
- **Main heat-spreader supplier to a US-based GPU maker** — a qualified, designed-in position in an AI bottleneck.
- **Exceptional economics**: gross **41.8%**, operating **32.0%**, net **26.5%**, **ROE 24.96%**.
- **Debt-light and cash-generative**: **29.4% debt ratio**, **NT$10.25bn cash**, operating cash flow above net income.
- **EPS NT$20.37 → NT$36.76** in three years; dividend **NT$6.0 → NT$21.72** in four.

**Weaknesses**
- **2026Q1 EPS flat** (NT$9.53 vs NT$9.59) while monthly revenue accelerated to **+58%**.
- **93.2× earnings and 23.34× book**, **0.64% yield** — no margin of safety, no income.
- **Customer concentration** in one large GPU programme.

**Opportunities**
- **Dayuan expansion 2025–2027**, floor area **+30%**, for high-end spreaders and IGBT liquid-cooling modules.
- Migration into **microchannel liquid cooling and integrated lids**, raising content per package.
- High-end spreaders shipped in small volume from 2025Q4, ramping into 2H 2026.

**Threats**
- **AI thermal design revisions** correcting the premium on high-basis heat spreaders.
- A pause in hyperscaler capital spending affecting the whole AI chain simultaneously.
- Competitors qualifying into the same packages as volumes justify a second source.

- **Earnings stopped growing while revenue accelerated (the immediate issue).** **2026Q1 EPS of NT$9.53 against NT$9.59** a year earlier, in a period when monthly revenue reached **+58%**. Mix, start-up costs on newly shipped high-end products, or pricing could each explain it — but at **93.2× earnings**, a company must convert revenue growth into profit growth, and last quarter it did not.
- **The valuation leaves nothing to chance.** **23.34× book** for a metal-forming business, with a **0.64% yield**. Even excellent execution may not be sufficient; anything less would be repriced sharply.
- **Thermal architecture is a moving target.** Industry coverage specifically flags that **revisions to AI thermal design could correct the premium** on high-specification heat spreaders. Direct-to-die cooling and integrated cold plates change what a spreader does. This is not a risk that capacity or cost control addresses.
- **Customer and programme concentration.** Being the principal heat-spreader supplier to one US GPU maker is the reason for the margins and the reason a single design decision or second-source qualification matters disproportionately.
- **The whole AI chain moves together.** Jentech's demand traces to hyperscaler capital spending — the same driver behind Elite Material, Taiwan Glass, King Slide, Wiwynn and Shihlin Electric in this collection. A capex pause would hit all of them at once.
- **The 2026 forecasts in circulation are analysts', not the company's.** Revenue of **NT$27.44bn** and EPS of **NT$52.1** are external estimates. They should not be read as guidance, and this page does not treat them as such.

Jentech's outlook rests on one question: **does the accelerating revenue start converting into earnings again?** The axes to watch:

- **EPS against the revenue line.** The decisive comparison. Monthly revenue reached **+58%** while **2026Q1 EPS was flat at NT$9.53**. If the second quarter shows earnings growing with revenue, the flat quarter was a mix or start-up effect; if the gap persists, the premium on heat spreaders is being competed or designed away.
- **Gross margin.** Held at **41.8%** in 2026Q1 within a **37.7–44.9%** band. This is the cleanest read on whether pricing power is intact as high-end products ramp.
- **The high-end ramp and Dayuan capacity.** Small-volume shipment began in **2025Q4** with a second-half 2026 ramp, against a **~30% floor-area expansion** through 2027. Utilisation and yield on the new products determine the margin.
- **Thermal architecture news.** Any move by AI chip designers toward direct-to-die or integrated cooling would change the heat spreader's role. This is external, unforecastable, and the most consequential risk to the current premium.
- **Full-year EPS against FY2025's NT$36.76.** The benchmark. Analyst estimates of **NT$52.1** are external projections, not guidance.

Bottom line: Jentech converted an **LED leadframe stamping business into the supplier of the heat spreader that sits on AI accelerators**, earning **41.8% gross and 32.0% operating margins**, **24.96% on equity**, with a **29.4% debt ratio**, **cash flow above profit**, and a dividend that rose from **NT$6.0 to NT$21.72** in four years. It is also a company whose **2026Q1 earnings were flat while revenue accelerated to +58%**, trading at **93.2× earnings and 23.34× book**, in a layer of the AI stack where **design revisions could correct the premium**. Judge it on **EPS growth relative to revenue and on gross margin** — a genuinely scarce position, at a price that has already assumed the next several years.
